Aldol condensation. A classic carbon-carbon bond-forming reaction in which an enol or enolate ion reacts with a carbonyl compound—an aldehyde or ketone—to form a beta-hydroxy carbonyl species, which often undergoes subsequent dehydration to yield a conjugated enone. It is a fundamental tool in organic chemistry used to build complex carbon frameworks.

The reaction requires acid or base catalysis to deprotonate the alpha-carbon of a carbonyl compound, generating a nucleophilic enolate ion or enol intermediate. The initial addition phase produces a beta-hydroxy aldehyde or beta-hydroxy ketone, named aldol as a portmanteau of aldehyde and alcohol. Upon heating, the reaction undergoes subsequent dehydration—the loss of water—to yield an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound, driven by the thermodynamic stability of the resulting conjugated pi system.

The reaction utilizes crossed aldol reactions between two different carbonyl compounds, which are most efficient when only one reactant has acidic alpha-hydrogens, such as benzaldehyde or formaldehyde, to prevent multiple self-condensation products. The reaction also proceeds intramolecularly to construct cyclic systems, forming stable five- or six-membered rings, which is the final step of the Robinson annulation sequence.

Aldehydes serve as common substrates for both enolate generation and nucleophilic attack in the reaction. Ketones undergo aldol reactions, though their equilibrium is generally less thermodynamically favorable than that of aldehydes due to steric and electronic factors. The elimination of water is the defining step that converts the aldol addition product into the final condensation product.
